subject: QuantifyAI: request for streaming delivery latency exception / pilot

Cc: procurement@quantify.ai
Date: Wed, 05 May 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Real-time co-pilot latency requirements / streaming SLA exception request

Hi Ava,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We have a short internal blocker before we can move forward with the pilot: our product team requires very tight time-to-first-byte and sustained token emission for the streaming API. Typical user flows are voice-driven and need the assistant to start speaking within ~100-200ms of request start and sustain ~50 tokens/sec during long responses.

Our questions:
- Can Redwood commit to a TTFT (time-to-first-token) of <= 200ms for streaming endpoints for our pilot (dedicated workload)?
- Can you guarantee sustained token/sec for long-running responses (60–120s) without progressive degradation?
- If not, what carveouts or dedicated configurations are available and how does that change pricing?

I've attached our SLO worksheet for the pilot. Procurement is on the Cc for contract scope / pricing.

Elena
Head of Platform
QuantifyAI

Attachments: QuantifyAI_SLO_requirements.xlsx

Hi Elena —

Appreciate the level of detail and the worksheet. Short answer: we can design a pilot to meet much tighter streaming delivery targets, but it will require a dedicated configuration (reserved capacity + warm worker pools) and an engineering validation run. By default our hosted streaming endpoints optimize for cost-efficiency (shared pools, dynamic batching) which can introduce non-deterministic TTFT at very low QPS.

Proposed next steps:
1) Internal review + engineering feasibility check (I've looped in Marissa and Ben).
2) We design a pilot config (dedicated pool, pinned concurrency, keepalives) and run a validation with a replay of your traffic shape.
3) If validation meets the thresholds, we attach a short MOU for the pilot priced as a dedicated capacity seat (we'll include uplift for warm standby).

Quick ask for your team: can you share 1 week of request traces (anonymized) and a sample of long-response prompts so Marissa's team can size CPU/GPU warm pools?

I’ll follow up with a technical note and the proposed config.

— Ava
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

From: marissa.cole@redwood.ai

Subject: Re: QuantifyAI: request for streaming delivery latency exception / pilot

Ava / Ben / Elena —

High-level engineering assessment after quick review of the worksheet and typical constraints:

1) Why streaming TTFT varies: our shared-hosted streaming relies on continuous batching and adaptive work assignment. At low QPS bursts, batching can introduce queueing delays that affect TTFT.

2) Options to tighten TTFT and sustain emission:
  - Dedicated reserved pool: allocate fixed GPU workers pinned to the tenant. This eliminates inter-tenant batching delays.
  - Warm standby + keepalives: keep KV caches hot and maintain resident processes for low-latency starts. That requires standby capacity (pricing uplift).
  - Minimum concurrency reserves: set a minimum number of in-use model instances to avoid cold-starts for long responses.

3) Practical SLOs for a Dedicated pilot (what we can guarantee after a validation run):
  - TTFT: median 120–250ms, 95th percentile <= 400ms (depends on model size and avg prompt length).
  - Sustained token emission: baseline 35–60 tokens/sec sustained; bursts up to 80–100 tokens/sec for short periods if autoscaling is allowed.
  - Long responses (60–120s): we can maintain emission rate within +/- 10% if the session is pinned to a worker and KV cache is provisioned.

4) Technical constraints / caveats:
  - Smaller models or quantized variants improve TTFT but may affect output quality.
  - Long websocket connections should use a short keepalive (30s) and we recommend a heartbeat to keep worker affinity.
  - If the customer routes some traffic to hosted shared endpoints, we cannot extend the same TTFT guarantees there.

5) Validation plan:
  - Customer provides 1 week of sanitized traces and representative long-response prompts.
  - We provision a dedicated pool and run a 48-hour replay test across peak/idle patterns and report TTFT percentiles and token/sec stability.

If this aligns, we can draft a pilot MOU with defined success metrics, pricing uplift for warm standby, and an exit criteria.

— Marissa
Sr. Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

Attachment: dedicated_config_proposal.pdf

From: ava.chen@redwood.ai

Cc: ben.carter@redwood.ai, marissa.cole@redwood.ai, procurement@quantify.ai
Date: Wed, 05 May 2027 12:10:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: QuantifyAI: request for streaming delivery latency exception / pilot — proposed carveout

Elena —

Thanks — Marissa's assessment is aligned with what our platform team recommends. To summarize the proposed carveout for the pilot:

- Infrastructure: Dedicated GPU pool + warm standby (pinned workers)
- Expected TTFT (post-validation): median 150ms, 95th <= 350ms (model dependent)
- Sustained token/sec: guaranteed 40 tokens/sec baseline for long responses, with headroom to 80 tokens/sec for short bursts
- Integration notes: use WebSocket streaming, implement 30s keepalive heartbeats, and avoid switching between hosted & dedicated for the same session to preserve affinity
- Pricing: dedicated pilot priced as a monthly reserved seat + 20–30% uplift for warm standby. Exact numbers to be included in MOU.

Next steps:
1) Elena — share traces and representative prompts (anonymized).
2) We provision the pilot config and run a 48-hour replay validation.
3) If metrics meet the agreed thresholds, we execute a pilot MOU (I'll loop procurement).

If Quantify agrees to the pilot outline I’ll send the DocuSign link for the MOU and schedule a 30-minute technical kickoff with Marissa.

— Ava
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
